name: Wendy Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the dairy on the hill road, on the yoghurt filling line. The machine fills the little pots, puts the foil lids on and seals them with heat, and I keep it fed with pots and foil, check the weights, check the seals, and stop the line if something goes wrong. We wear hairnets and white boots and the room is kept cold, so I wear two jumpers under my coat even in summer. I like that it's clean and that I know the women on my shift, and I don't love the five a.m. starts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been at the dairy?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two years. Before that I worked in my parents' bakery for twenty years, until the big supermarket opened and the bakery closed. So I'm the new one again, still learning the filler, and the line leader, Rosa, keeps an eye on me. My husband Paulo is a plumber, he works for himself, so some months are good and some aren't. Our daughter Beatriz is thirteen and Luca is nine. We sing in the church choir on Sundays, and between the mortgage and Paulo's van there's never more than a few weeks of money put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh, good. That would be a relief, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you go, the world keeps turning. People need yoghurt and somebody has to make it. I'd say that at work and to the ladies in the choir, I'm not one for posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job and get better at it. I'd like to be the one Rosa doesn't have to check. That's about it, really. I've had my share of big changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Ask Rosa to teach me the changeovers. Use the chatbot thing Beatriz set up on my phone for meal plans now and then, it helps with the budget. Nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the chatbot helps with the budget. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tell it what's in the cupboard and how much I've got for the week, and it gives me meals. Last week it was a lentil thing the kids actually ate. Paulo said it was the best thing the robot ever did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned big changes. Do you mean the bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. My father cried the day we closed. Forty years of getting up at three. The supermarket sells bread for half what we could, and it's not as good, but people buy it. I learned then that good isn't always enough.

S0.say: There you go, the world keeps turning. People need yoghurt and somebody has to make it, and I'd say that at work and to the ladies in the choir.
S0.think: It means I keep my job and get better at it, so Rosa doesn't have to check me. I've had my share of big changes already.
S0.do: Keeps going and asks the line leader to teach her changeovers. Uses the chatbot her daughter set up now and then for budget meal plans.
S0.quote: I learned then that good isn't always enough.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy has already lived through her family bakery being beaten by a supermarket, and it shapes her view that quality doesn't protect you. She uses AI tools lightly for practical home tasks. In the flat scenario she just wants to get good at her job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mm. That sounds like what happened to the bakery, only everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say you have to roll up your sleeves and learn, there's no use moaning. Companies should offer proper training, apprenticeships even for older people, and families should help each other through it. I wouldn't want the government running everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a bit worried. They already have a new line in the other hall where a robot packs the pots into trays. I'm junior and still slow. But if they show me how, I'll learn, I learned the bakery ovens and I learned this. I just need someone to show me properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see if the new machines actually work, then put my name down for training once a few of the girls had done it. I'd ask Rosa which skills they'd need. I'd use the chatbot a bit more to understand things. And we'd tighten up at home a little, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. But I'd manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said families should help each other through it. What would that look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paulo's brother has a bathroom fitting business, he's always short of hands. My mum would watch the kids if I had to do a course. That's what family is for. We did it when the bakery closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa, actually. She's sixty and she's the one who knows everything, but she hates computers. If the new line needs a tablet for everything, she'll be miserable. I'd try to help her the way she helps me.

S1.say: You have to roll up your sleeves and learn; there's no use moaning. Companies should offer proper training, apprenticeships even for older people, and families should help each other through it.
S1.think: I'm a bit worried, because there's already a robot packing pots in the other hall and I'm junior and slow. But if someone shows me properly, I'll learn, like I learned the bakery ovens and this machine.
S1.do: Waits until the new machines prove themselves, then signs up for training once colleagues have. Uses the chatbot a bit more to understand things and tightens the household budget slightly.
S1.feel: A little uneasy but confident she'd manage.
S1.quote: I'd try to help her the way she helps me.
S1.fieldNote: Wendy is a classic follower on new tech: she'd train once others had shown it works. Her safety net is family, not the state: her brother-in-law's business and her mother's childcare. She thinks of her line leader's struggles with computers as much as her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Oh dear. That's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to pull together as families and communities, and pray. I'd say businesses and government should have seen it coming. I'd tell people at church we'll have to look after each other more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, I think I'd be out of the dairy within a year. And Paulo's plumbing, if robots can do hands-on work, how long does that last? People might want a person in their house for a while, but would they pay for one? We have a few weeks of money. That's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back right away, no extras, no new school shoes until they're needed, the car stays parked. I'd go and help Paulo with his business, do his books and phone calls properly so he gets more jobs, because that's the one thing we own. I'd ask my parents and the church if we needed help, I wouldn't be too proud. And I'd still keep my job as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Waking up at night thinking about the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't be too proud to ask for help. Was that always true?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. When the bakery closed I didn't want anyone to know we were struggling. Then the ladies from church brought food, and I cried, and I realised that's what it's for. I'd ask sooner now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Beatriz and Luca?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd be all right because we have each other and God. And that they'd have to help more at home. Beatriz would understand. Luca would ask if he can still have his birthday party.

S2.say: We have to pull together as families and communities, and pray. Businesses and government should have seen it coming, and at church we'd look after each other more than ever.
S2.think: I think I'd be out of the dairy within a year, and I'm not sure how long Paulo's plumbing lasts if robots do hands-on work. We only have a few weeks of money.
S2.do: Cuts all extras and parks the car, and does her husband's books and phone calls to win him more jobs. Asks her parents and church for help early and keeps her dairy job as long as she can.
S2.feel: Scared and waking at night over the mortgage.
S2.quote: Then the ladies from church brought food, and I cried, and I realised that's what it's for.
S2.fieldNote: With two years, Wendy pivots straight to the one thing the family owns, Paulo's plumbing business. The bakery closure taught her to ask for help sooner, which she says openly. Her faith and church community are her main safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's better. Still not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift if we use it. Families should save, kids should learn trades, and companies should train people up. I wouldn't wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd use the time to really learn the business side of Paulo's work, the bookings and the accounts, and maybe build it up so it's a family business. And save. If people still want a person to fix their boiler, that's where we'd be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a bookkeeping course at the college in the evenings, once I saw it was worth it, and use the chatbot to help me with the homework. I'd start doing Paulo's paperwork and save every bit extra. I'd keep working at the dairy until the business could pay me. I'd think about what Beatriz studies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd feel useful. I'm better when I'm busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said "once I saw it was worth it". How would you know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my cousin Ana, she did one last year and now she does books for three shops. If she says it's worth it, I'd do it. I always like to see somebody else do it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Paulo feel about you running the business side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, honestly. He hates the paperwork. He keeps receipts in a shoebox in the van. He'd say "you're the boss now", and he'd only half be joking.

S3.say: Five years is a gift if we use it: families should save, kids should learn trades and companies should train people up. I wouldn't wait for the government.
S3.think: I'd use the time to learn the business side of Paulo's plumbing and build it into a family business, and save. If people still want a person to fix their boiler, that's where we'd be.
S3.do: Takes an evening bookkeeping course once her cousin confirms it's worthwhile, and studies with the chatbot. Takes over her husband's paperwork, saves every extra and stays at the dairy until the business can pay her.
S3.quote: He keeps receipts in a shoebox in the van.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Wendy turn her husband's trade into a family business plan. She still waits for proof from someone she trusts before committing. The family business fits her traditional values neatly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be fifty-three. Luca would be nineteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to prepare properly. Raise your children right, learn a trade, save, and look after your neighbours. I'd say that at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels manageable. I'd have the bookkeeping, we'd have built up Paulo's business, the kids would be grown. The end still worries me, because if robots do everything, even the business goes. But we'd have had ten good years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do the bookkeeping course properly, build up the family business, save a bit every month. Help Beatriz choose something sensible, maybe nursing or a trade. Learn the AI tools a bit more once I see others using them for business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A little uneasy about the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Beatriz to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She wants to be a vet. I'd say lovely, go for it, animals need people. I just don't want her to pick something where she sits at a computer, because I think the computer will do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn AI tools for the business. Isn't that the same thing that might take the business away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I suppose. But that's how it was with the bakery: the shops that got the new ovens lasted longer. I'd rather be using it than be beaten by it.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to prepare properly. Raise your children right, learn a trade, save and look after your neighbours, and I'd say that at church.
S4.think: Ten years feels manageable: I'd have the bookkeeping, Paulo's business built up and the kids grown. The end still worries me, but we'd have had ten good years.
S4.do: Completes the bookkeeping course and builds up the family plumbing business while saving monthly. Guides her daughter towards sensible, people-facing work and learns AI tools for the business once others prove them.
S4.feel: Mostly okay, slightly uneasy about the end.
S4.quote: I'd rather be using it than be beaten by it.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years makes Wendy's family business plan feel solid. She draws directly on the bakery lesson that those who adopted new tools lasted longer. She steers her daughter away from computer-based work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There'd be no time to build anything. What would help is help with the mortgage for a while, and making it easy for small family businesses like Paulo's to keep going, less paperwork and fewer fees.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my parents. They lost their bakery to a big company. If this happens, it's the same story for everybody, just bigger.

headlineQuote: If this happens, it's the same story for everybody, just bigger.
portrait: Wendy is forty-three and has worked on a yoghurt filling line at a dairy for two years, after twenty years in her parents' bakery until a supermarket put it out of business. She's a churchgoer who trusts family and community over government and uses a chatbot now and then for meal planning. She adopts new things once others have shown they work. Fast AGI alarms her, but with more time she'd build her plumber husband's trade into a family business, drawing on the lesson that those who adopted new tools lasted longer.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to build up the family business and only a few weeks of savings.
whatWouldHelp: Help with the mortgage for a while, and less paperwork and fewer fees for small family businesses like her husband's.
